entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12040"/><div sID="gen21771" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12040"/><hi type="bold">2. whiles he tasted the wine--</hi>While under the effects of wine, men will do what they dare not do when sober.<div eID="gen21771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21772" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his father Nebuchadnezzar--</hi>that is, his forefather. So "Jesus ... the son of David, the son of Abraham" (<reference osisRef="Matt.1.1">Mt 1:1</reference>). Daniel does not say that the other kings mentioned in other writers did not reign between Belshazzar and Nebuchadnezzar, namely, Evil-merodach (<reference osisRef="Jer.52.31">Jr 52:31</reference>), Neriglissar, his brother-in-law, and Laborasoarchod (nine months). Berosus makes Nabonidus, the last king, to have been one of the people, raised to the throne by an insurrection. As the inscriptions show that Belshazzar was distinct from, and joint king with, him, this is not at variance with Daniel, whose statement that Belshazzar was son (grandson) of Nebuchadnezzar is corroborated by Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.27.7">Jr 27:7</reference>). Their joint, yet independent, testimony, as contemporaries, and having the best means of information, is more trustworthy than any of the heathen historians, if there were a discrepancy. Evil-merodach, son of Nebuchadnezzar (according to Berosus), reigned but a short time (one or two years), having, in consequence of his bad government, been dethroned by a plot of Neriglissar, his sister's husband; hence Daniel does not mention him. At the elevation of Nabonidus as supreme king, Belshazzar, the grandson of Nebuchadnezzar, was doubtless suffered to be subordinate king and successor, in order to conciliate the legitimate party. Thus the seeming discrepancy becomes a confirmation of genuineness when cleared up, for the real harmony must have been undesigned.<div eID="gen21772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21773" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wives ... concubines--</hi>not usually present at feasts in the East, where women of the harem are kept in strict seclusion. Hence Vashti's refusal to appear at Ahasuerus' feast (<reference osisRef="Esth.1.9-Esth.1.12">Es 1:9-12</reference>). But the Babylonian court, in its reckless excesses, seems not to have been so strict as the Persian. Xenophon [Cyropædia, 5.2,28] confirms Daniel, representing a feast of Belshazzar where the concubines are present. At the beginning "the lords" (<reference osisRef="Dan.5.1">Da 5:1</reference>), for whom the feast was made, alone seem to have been present; but as the revelry advanced, the women were introduced. Two classes of them are mentioned, those to whom belonged the privileges of "wives," and those strictly concubines (<reference osisRef="2Sam.5.13">2Sa 5:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.3">1Ki 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.6.8">So 6:8</reference>). <div eID="gen21773" type="x-p"/>

She was wife either of Nebuchadnezzar or of Evil merodach; hence her acquaintance with the services of Daniel. She completed the great works which the former had begun. Hence Herodotus attributes them to her alone. This accounts for the deference paid to her by Belshazzar. (See on <reference osisRef="Dan.4.36">Da 4:36</reference>). Compare similar rank given to the queen mother among the Hebrews (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.13">1Ki 15:13</reference>). <div eID="gen21786" type="x-p"/>

The honors in <reference osisRef="Dan.5.29">Da 5:29</reference> were doubtless urged on him, without his wish, in such a way that he could not with propriety refuse them. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12061"/><div sID="gen21808" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12061"/><hi type="bold">29. Belshazzar ... clothed Daniel with scarlet--</hi>To come from the presence of a prince in a dress presented to the wearer as a distinction is still held a great honor in the East. Daniel was thus restored to a similar rank to what he had held under Nebuchadnezzar (<reference osisRef="Dan.2.48">Da 2:48</reference>). Godly fidelity which might be expected to bring down vengeance, as in this case, is often rewarded even in this life. The king, having promised, was ashamed before his courtiers to break his word. He perhaps also affected to despise the prophecy of his doom, as an idle threat. As to Daniel's reasons for now accepting what at first he had declined, compare Note, see on <reference osisRef="Dan.5.17">Da 5:17</reference>. The insignia of honor would be witnesses for God's glory to the world of his having by God's aid interpreted the mystic characters. The cause of his elevation too would secure the favor of the new dynasty (<reference osisRef="Dan.6.2">Da 6:2</reference>) for both himself and his captive countrymen. As the capture of the city by Cyrus was not till near daylight, there was no want of time in that eventful night for accomplishing all that is here recorded. The capture of the city so immediately after the prophecy of it (following Belshazzar's sacrilege), marked most emphatically to the whole world the connection between Babylon's sin and its punishment. <div eID="gen21808" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12062"/><div sID="gen21809" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12062"/>30. Herodotus and Xenophon confirm Daniel as to the suddenness of the event. Cyrus diverted the Euphrates into a new channel and, guided by two deserters, marched by the dry bed into the city, while the Babylonians were carousing at an annual feast to the gods. See also <reference osisRef="Isa.21.5">Is 21:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.27">44:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.50.38">Jr 50:38</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.50.39">39</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.51.36">51:36</reference>. As to Belshazzar's being slain, compare Is 14:18-20; 21:2-9; Jr 50:29-35; 51:57. <div eID="gen21809" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv12063"/><div sID="gen21810" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv12063"/><hi type="bold">31. Darius the Median--</hi>that is, Cyaxares II, the son and successor of Astyages, 569-536 B.C. Though Koresh, or Cyrus, was leader of the assault, yet all was done in the name of Darius; therefore, he alone is mentioned here; but <reference osisRef="Dan.6.28">Da 6:28</reference> shows Daniel was not ignorant of Cyrus' share in the capture of Babylon. <reference osisRef="Isa.13.17">Is 13:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.21.2">21:2</reference>, confirm Daniel in making the Medes the leading nation in destroying Babylon. So also <reference osisRef="Jer.51.11">Jr 51:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.28">28</reference>. Herodotus, on the other hand, omits mentioning Darius, as that king, being weak and sensual, gave up all the authority to his energetic nephew, Cyrus [Xenophon, Cyropædia, 1.5; 8.7].<div eID="gen21810" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21811" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">threescore and two years old--</hi>This agrees with Xenophon [Cyropædia, 8.5,19], as to Cyaxares II.  <chapter eID="Dan.5"/>
entries.content_plain: 31. Darius the Median-- that is, Cyaxares II, the son and successor of Astyages, 569-536 B.C. Though Koresh, or Cyrus, was leader of the assault, yet all was done in the name of Darius; therefore, he alone is mentioned here; but Da 6:28 shows Daniel was not ignorant of Cyrus' share in the capture of Babylon. Is 13:17 ; 21:2 , confirm Daniel in making the Medes the leading nation in destroying Babylon. So also Jr 51:11 , 28 . Herodotus, on the other hand, omits mentioning Darius, as that king, being weak and sensual, gave up all the authority to his energetic nephew, Cyrus [Xenophon, Cyropædia, 1.5; 8.7]. threescore and two years old-- This agrees with Xenophon [Cyropædia, 8.5,19], as to Cyaxares II.
